Internationalization & Localization.text: Rocket.Chat's i18n architecture is split across two layers: a shared TypeScript package (`pkg:i18n`) that owns type definitions and utility logic, and a Meteor-level package (`pkg:rocketchat-i18n`) that bootstraps translation files at application startup. These two layers are bridged at runtime by a React provider on the client side and a server-side i18n module.

The canonical set of valid translation key identifiers is defined in `packages/i18n/src/resources.ts`. This file exports the `RocketchatI18nKeys` type, a union that enumerates every permissible key string across all Rocket.Chat subsystems. By encoding all keys as a TypeScript type, the codebase gains compile-time safety: any reference to a non-existent key becomes a type error rather than a silent runtime miss.

Sources: packages/i18n/src/resources.ts:L1

The core utilities live in `packages/i18n/src/index.ts`, which exports three primary symbols:

- **`addSprinfToI18n`** — Augments an i18next-compatible instance with `sprintf`-style interpolation, allowing translation strings to use positional `%s` / `%d` placeholders in addition to the default named-key interpolation.
- **`extractTranslationNamespaces`** — Parses a flat translation resource object and splits it into named namespaces, enabling lazy loading of only the namespace a feature needs.
- **`extractTranslationKeys`** — Walks a namespace-partitioned resource and returns a flat array of qualified key strings, used during build-time validation and tooling.
- **`TranslationNamespace`** — A TypeScript type that constrains namespace identifiers to those actually present in the resource bundle.

Sources: packages/i18n/src/index.ts:L1

Together, these utilities enforce namespace discipline: features declare a namespace, load only its keys, and reference them through typed accessors backed by `RocketchatI18nKeys`.

The `apps/meteor/packages/rocketchat-i18n/package.js` file configures the Meteor build system to discover all `.json` translation files in the application tree and register them as Meteor assets. At startup, the package iterates these assets and feeds them into the i18n runtime, making every locale available without a separate HTTP fetch per locale on the server.

Sources: apps/meteor/packages/rocketchat-i18n/package.js:L1

This Meteor-level integration is intentionally thin: it handles file discovery and asset registration but delegates all key resolution and interpolation logic to the `pkg:i18n` utilities described above.

On the browser, `apps/meteor/client/providers/TranslationProvider.tsx` wires the translation system into the React tree. It exports two cooperating pieces:

- **`useI18next`** — A hook that initializes and returns a configured i18next instance, applying `addSprinfToI18n` to extend it with sprintf support.
- **`TranslationProviderInner`** — A component that consumes the i18next instance from `useI18next`, wraps children in the standard i18next React context, and handles locale change subscriptions so the UI re-renders when a user switches language.

Sources: apps/meteor/client/providers/TranslationProvider.tsx:L1

Namespace splitting handled by `extractTranslationNamespaces` is exploited here: `TranslationProviderInner` can load namespaces on demand rather than shipping the entire bundle to the client upfront.

`apps/meteor/server/lib/i18n.ts` provides the server-equivalent singleton. It initializes i18next in a Node.js context, loads locale files from the assets registered by the Meteor package, and exposes translation helpers used by server-side code paths such as notification text generation and email templates.

Sources: apps/meteor/server/lib/i18n.ts:L1

Each sub-package carries its own Jest configuration. The `pkg:i18n` package uses `packages/i18n/jest.config.ts` to run unit tests against the utility functions in isolation, independent of Meteor or browser globals.

Sources: packages/i18n/jest.config.ts:L1

HTTP Router, REST API & Type Contracts.section: HTTP Router, REST API & Type Contracts
HTTP Router, REST API & Type Contracts.text:
This chapter describes how Rocket.Chat structures its HTTP routing layer, exposes REST endpoints, and enforces type contracts across the request/response lifecycle. The system is built around a Hono-based router with an Express adapter, a rich set of TypeScript type definitions, and AJV-powered runtime validation.

---

The core routing infrastructure lives in the `http-router` package. The `definition.ts` file establishes the foundational type vocabulary: `Range`, `SuccessStatusCodes`, and `RedirectStatusCodes` are defined here as typed enumerations that constrain which HTTP status codes may appear in route handler return values.

Sources: packages/http-router/src/definition.ts:L1

The `Router` class in the same package bridges the Express and Hono frameworks. It exposes `registerTypedRoutes` for declarative, type-safe route registration and `parseBodyParams` for normalizing incoming request bodies. The class uses `convertActionToHandler` internally to wrap typed Hono action functions into Express-compatible handlers.

Sources: packages/http-router/src/Router.ts:L1

The Express adapter is provided by `honoAdapterForExpress`, a middleware factory that allows Hono route handlers to be mounted directly into an Express application. This adapter is the integration seam that lets the new Hono-based routing layer coexist with the existing Meteor/Express infrastructure.

Sources: packages/http-router/src/middlewares/honoAdapterForExpress.ts:L1

Query string parsing is handled by `parseQueryParams`, a thin utility built on the `qs` library. It normalizes URL query strings into structured objects, matching the conventions expected by Express middleware and downstream route handlers.

Sources: packages/http-router/src/parseQueryParams.ts:L1

---

HTTP Router, REST API & Type Contracts.section: REST API Initialization and Route Definitions
HTTP Router, REST API & Type Contracts.text:
The main REST API surface is initialized in `apps/meteor/app/api/server/api.ts`, which sets up Express routers, applies default rate-limiting options, and wires reactive settings watchers that can modify API behavior at runtime. This file exports the `API` singleton used throughout the server layer.

Sources: apps/meteor/app/api/server/api.ts:L1

Route handler types are codified in `apps/meteor/app/api/server/definition.ts`, which defines TypeScript interfaces for API route handlers, HTTP response shapes, and request execution contexts. These types ensure that endpoint implementations conform to a consistent contract.

Sources: apps/meteor/app/api/server/definition.ts:L1

---

The `rest-typings` package provides the shared type contracts consumed by both server and client code. `PaginatedRequest` defines the optional `count`, `offset`, `sort`, and `fields` parameters that paginated endpoints accept.

Sources: packages/rest-typings/src/helpers/PaginatedRequest.ts:L1

`PaginatedResult` is the complementary response type, carrying `count`, `offset`, and `total` metadata alongside the result payload. These two types form the canonical pagination contract across all REST endpoints.

Sources: packages/rest-typings/src/helpers/PaginatedResult.ts:L1

For federation endpoints, `FederationPaginatedRequest` and `FederationPaginatedResult` re-export and extend the base pagination types to accommodate federation-specific query parameters.

Sources: packages/rest-typings/src/v1/federation/index.ts:L1

Group-based endpoints use `withGroupBaseProperties`, `baseSchema`, and `withBaseProps` — factory functions that compose AJV-compatible JSON schemas and TypeScript types for request properties shared across group operations.

Sources: packages/rest-typings/src/v1/groups/BaseProps.ts:L1

---

HTTP Router, REST API & Type Contracts.section: AJV Validation and Error Response Schemas
HTTP Router, REST API & Type Contracts.text:
Runtime request validation is centralized in `packages/rest-typings/src/v1/Ajv.ts`. This module configures a shared AJV instance and exports pre-compiled validators: `validateBadRequestErrorResponse`, `validateUnauthorizedErrorResponse`, and `validateForbiddenErrorResponse`. These validators are used across endpoint handlers to assert that error payloads conform to the expected schema before sending them to clients.

Sources: packages/rest-typings/src/v1/Ajv.ts:L1

---

Enterprise endpoints are layered on top of the base API in `apps/meteor/ee/server/api/api.ts`. This middleware enforces two-factor authentication requirements when no valid enterprise license is detected, acting as a gate before any enterprise route handler executes.

Sources: apps/meteor/ee/server/api/api.ts:L1

Concrete enterprise endpoints include receipt retrieval for messages (`chat.ts`), LDAP synchronization triggers (`ldap.ts`), audit room member queries (`audit.ts`), and custom role management (`roles.ts`). Each follows the same pattern: validate the request shape, check permissions, and delegate to a service layer.

Sources: apps/meteor/ee/server/api/chat.ts:L1
Sources: apps/meteor/ee/server/api/ldap.ts:L1
Sources: apps/meteor/ee/server/api/audit.ts:L1
Sources: apps/meteor/ee/server/api/roles.ts:L1

---

The HTTP routing and REST API layer forms a layered stack: Hono route definitions and Express adapters at the transport layer, typed handler contracts in the API definition module, shared pagination and schema types in `rest-typings`, AJV validators for runtime safety, and enterprise middleware for license-gated features. This architecture ensures end-to-end type safety from URL parameter parsing through to serialized HTTP responses.

Job Scheduling, Agenda & Queue Worker.text:
This chapter describes the background job scheduling infrastructure in Rocket.Chat, covering the core Agenda scheduler library, the shared cron abstraction package, and the enterprise queue-worker microservice.

---

Rocket.Chat's background job system is built around a MongoDB-backed scheduler called **Agenda**, exposed through a shared `@rocket.chat/cron` package that provides a stable, singleton interface for the rest of the platform. An optional enterprise microservice (`queue-worker`) consumes jobs from this infrastructure for isolated, scalable background processing.

---

The Agenda package is the lowest-level scheduling primitive. Its central class, `Agenda`, manages MongoDB persistence, job registration, concurrency limits, and the polling loop that dispatches due jobs.

Sources: packages/agenda/src/Agenda.ts:L1

### Job Model

Each scheduled task is represented by a `Job` instance. The `Job` class holds all mutable state for a scheduled unit of work, including its next run time, failure count, and execution result. Key methods include:

- `toJSON` — serializes job attributes for storage.
- `computeNextRunAt` — calculates the next execution timestamp, delegating to either `_computeFromInterval` (for repeating jobs on a fixed cadence) or `_computeFromRepeat` (for cron-expression-based jobs).
- `fail` — records an error against the job record, incrementing the failure count and storing the error message.

Sources: packages/agenda/src/Job.ts:L1

### Type Definitions

The scheduling system uses a layered type hierarchy. `IJob`, `IJobAttributes`, and `IJobRecord` define the runtime shape of a job and its persisted form, separating the in-memory representation from the MongoDB document structure.

Sources: packages/agenda/src/definition/IJob.ts:L1

Job registration is typed through `JobDefinition` and `JobOptions`, which describe the handler function signature, concurrency settings, and locking semantics that `Agenda` uses when defining a new job kind.

Sources: packages/agenda/src/definition/JobDefinition.ts:L1

### Utilities

The `noCallback` utility normalizes the argument list of functions that optionally accept a Node.js-style callback, inserting a no-op when the caller omits one. This keeps internal job handlers consistent regardless of calling convention.

Sources: packages/agenda/src/lib/noCallback.ts:L1

The `createJob` factory function instantiates a `Job` from raw MongoDB document data, binding it to its parent `Agenda` instance. This is the standard path by which the scheduler rehydrates persisted job records on startup or after a poll.

Sources: packages/agenda/src/createJob.ts:L1

---

The `@rocket.chat/cron` package wraps `Agenda` in a higher-level singleton class, `AgendaCronJobs`, which is the interface used by server-side application code. It exposes:

- `start` — initializes the Agenda connection and begins the polling loop.
- `add` — registers a named recurring job with a cron expression.
- `addAtTimestamp` — schedules a one-shot job to run at a specific moment.
- `remove` — cancels and removes a named job.
- `has`, `reserve`, and `unreserve` — provide cooperative locking semantics to prevent duplicate execution in multi-instance deployments.

Sources: packages/cron/src/index.ts:L1

This singleton design means that any server-side module can import `AgendaCronJobs` and schedule work without needing to manage its own Agenda connection, reducing the risk of duplicate schedulers and connection leaks.

---

The `queue-worker` is an enterprise-tier microservice that offloads compute-intensive or latency-sensitive background jobs from the main Rocket.Chat process. Its entry point is `service.ts`, which bootstraps the service runtime and connects it to the shared job infrastructure.

Sources: ee/apps/queue-worker/src/service.ts:L1

---

Job Scheduling, Agenda & Queue Worker.section: Presence Reaping as a Representative Consumer
Job Scheduling, Agenda & Queue Worker.text:
The `PresenceReaper` in the enterprise presence package illustrates the end-to-end pattern: it registers a periodic job via `AgendaCronJobs`, and on each tick calls `processDocument` to evaluate individual session records and `flushBatch` to commit removals in bulk, minimizing write amplification.

Sources: ee/packages/presence/src/lib/PresenceReaper.ts:L1

This pattern — register with cron, process in batches, flush atomically — is the recommended architecture for any new background maintenance task in Rocket.Chat.

Microservice Network & Authorization Ser.text: This chapter describes how Rocket.Chat's enterprise tier externalizes authentication and permission enforcement into dedicated microservices—the **account-service** and **authorization-service**—that operate independently of the main Meteor process and communicate through the shared service API layer.

The core Meteor monolith handles the majority of user interactions, but high-frequency operations such as session validation and permission checks become bottlenecks at scale. The enterprise microservice network extracts these hot paths into autonomous Node.js services, each exposing a well-defined interface through `packages/core-services`, which publishes proxified service interfaces consumed across the codebase.

Sources: packages/core-services/src/index.ts:L1

The account-service owns the full lifecycle of user login sessions. It provides four primary operations: token generation, session persistence, session resumption, and session removal.

**Token generation** is handled by utility functions in `ee/apps/account-service/src/lib/utils.ts`. The module exports `getPassword`, `_generateStampedLoginToken`, `_hashLoginToken`, `_hashStampedToken`, and `validatePassword`. A stamped token couples a random token value with an expiry timestamp (`_tokenExpiration`) into an `IStampedToken` structure, ensuring tokens are time-bounded and cryptographically hashed before storage.

Sources: ee/apps/account-service/src/lib/utils.ts:L1

**Session persistence** is delegated to `saveSession`, which writes the hashed stamped token into the users collection so that subsequent resume attempts can validate against it.

Sources: ee/apps/account-service/src/lib/saveSession.ts:L1

**Resume authentication** is the hot path for reconnecting clients. `loginViaResume` accepts a resume token from the client, hashes it using the same deterministic algorithm, and queries the database for a matching session record. If found, it returns the associated user context to the caller.

Sources: ee/apps/account-service/src/lib/loginViaResume.ts:L1

**Session removal** is handled by `removeSession`, which invalidates a specific login token for a user, effectively logging out a single session without affecting other active sessions.

Sources: ee/apps/account-service/src/lib/removeSession.ts:L1

The REST API authentication contract is defined in `packages/rest-typings/src/v1/auth.ts`, which exports TypeScript types (`Password`, `isLoginProps`) and AJV validators for the `/v1/login` and `/v1/logout` endpoints. These types are consumed both by the Meteor API layer and the account-service to ensure consistent payload shapes across process boundaries.

Sources: packages/rest-typings/src/v1/auth.ts:L1

The `packages/account-utils` package provides a shared `hashLoginToken` function used symmetrically by both the account-service and the Meteor monolith. This ensures that a token hashed in one process can be validated in another without sharing secret state.

Sources: packages/account-utils/src/index.ts:L1

The authorization-service is surfaced to the rest of the codebase through the `Authorization` export from the core-services registry. Other services and the Meteor layer call permission-check methods through this proxy without knowing whether the authorization logic executes in-process or in a remote microservice.

Sources: packages/core-services/src/index.ts:L1

The queue-worker service (`ee/apps/queue-worker/src/service.ts`) is representative of how enterprise microservices initialize: they bootstrap infrastructure, register with the service mesh, and then begin consuming work. Each microservice follows the same entry-point pattern—singleton initialization followed by lifecycle event registration.

Sources: ee/apps/queue-worker/src/service.ts:L1

A typical resume-based authentication request flows as follows: the DDP client sends a resume token → the account-service's `loginViaResume` hashes the token → the hashed value is looked up via the database model layer (`BaseRaw.update` for token rotation) → a valid session returns the user record → downstream services query `Authorization` for permission checks through the core-services proxy. This separation keeps the Meteor process free of session-validation load while maintaining a single source of truth for user state.

Sources: ee/apps/account-service/src/lib/loginViaResume.ts:L1
Sources: packages/core-services/src/index.ts:L1

Client SDK, API Client & Shared Utilitie.section: Client SDK, API Client & Shared Utilities
Client SDK, API Client & Shared Utilitie.text:
This chapter describes the REST API client library, credential management, middleware pipeline, shared utility functions, and common error types that form the foundational layer for all client-to-server communication in Rocket.Chat.

---

The `RestClientInterface` defines the typed contract for all HTTP interactions between the client and server. It declares the `get`, `post`, `put`, and `delete` method signatures with full TypeScript generics, ensuring that every endpoint's request and response shapes are statically verified at compile time. The interface also introduces the `Middleware` and `Next` types, which compose a pipeline allowing cross-cutting concerns (such as authentication injection or TOTP challenge handling) to intercept requests before they are dispatched.

Sources: packages/api-client/src/RestClientInterface.ts:L1

The concrete implementation, `RestClient`, fulfills this interface and provides the actual HTTP transport. It exposes `getCredentials`, `getCredentialsAsHeaders`, and a low-level `send` method used internally by all verb-specific helpers. The class is exported from the package index as both a singleton and a reusable service class.

Sources: packages/api-client/src/index.ts:L1

---

Authentication state is encapsulated by the `Credentials` type, which models the `X-User-Id` and `X-Auth-Token` HTTP headers that Rocket.Chat's REST API requires on authenticated requests. By isolating credentials into a dedicated type module, the rest of the SDK can reference this contract without importing transport logic.

Sources: packages/api-client/src/Credentials.ts:L1

---

The `errors` module in `api-client` provides three exported type guards used throughout the authentication flow:

- **`isTotpRequiredError`** — identifies responses where the server demands a TOTP challenge before proceeding.
- **`isTotpInvalidError`** — identifies responses where a supplied TOTP code was rejected.
- **`isTwoFactorMethod`** / **`hasRequiredTwoFactorMethod`** — discriminate the specific 2FA method the server requires, enabling the client to route to the correct challenge UI.

Sources: packages/api-client/src/errors.ts:L1

A parallel set of client-side type guards in `apps/meteor/client/lib/2fa/utils.ts` extends this with `isTotpMaxAttemptsError`, covering the rate-limiting case that the API-client package does not model.

Sources: apps/meteor/client/lib/2fa/utils.ts:L1

---

Two modules maintain centralized registries of external URLs. The root-level `apps/meteor/client/lib/links.ts` serves as the canonical registry for documentation and product links used across the Meteor application, built around the `GO_ROCKET_CHAT_PREFIX` constant.

Sources: apps/meteor/client/lib/links.ts:L1

An equivalent registry exists in the UI client package at `packages/ui-client/src/lib/links.ts`, exposing the same `links` object as a singleton so that reusable UI components can resolve external URLs without a dependency on the Meteor application layer.

Sources: packages/ui-client/src/lib/links.ts:L1

---

Shared numeric and string constants (notification attachment colors, upload file limits, etc.) are co-located in `apps/meteor/lib/constants.ts`. Centralizing these values prevents magic-number drift across the monorepo and allows both client and server modules to import from a single authoritative source.

Sources: apps/meteor/lib/constants.ts:L1

---

The `CloudWorkspaceConnectionError` class provides a typed, named error for failures that occur when the workspace cannot reach Rocket.Chat Cloud services. By extending the standard `Error` prototype with a distinct class, upstream catch blocks can use `instanceof` checks rather than string-matching error messages.

Sources: apps/meteor/lib/errors/CloudWorkspaceConnectionError.ts:L1

The ABAC (Attribute-Based Access Control) subsystem defines its own error hierarchy in `ee/packages/abac/src/errors.ts`, including `AbacError`, `AbacInvalidAttributeValuesError`, and `AbacInvalidAttributeKeyError`. These errors carry structured `code` properties, enabling fine-grained error handling in permission enforcement paths.

Sources: ee/packages/abac/src/errors.ts:L1

---

Small, pure utility functions are distributed across the `apps/meteor/lib/` subtree. `getUserEmailAddress` extracts a user's primary email from a user object, while `getUserDisplayNames` formats display name arrays according to server-configured preferences. Both are hot-path utilities consumed broadly by UI and data layers.

Sources: apps/meteor/lib/getUserEmailAddress.ts:L1
Sources: apps/meteor/lib/getUserDisplayNames.ts:L1

The `isObject` type guard provides a lightweight check for plain-object values, underpinning validation logic in serialization and form-handling code.

Sources: apps/meteor/lib/utils/isObject.ts:L1

Crypto, Random & General-Purpose Package.text:
This chapter documents the lightweight, utility-focused packages that underpin cryptographic operations, random number generation, data encoding, and general-purpose helpers across the Rocket.Chat monorepo. These packages are deliberately narrow in scope, maximally reusable, and carry no framework dependencies.

---

The random package is built around the `RandomGenerator` class, which exposes a composable API for producing unpredictable values. Its primary entry point is `RandomGenerator`, which provides the `fraction`, `hexString`, and `insecure` surface areas.

Sources: packages/random/jest.config.ts:L1

The core primitive is an Alea-based generator. `createAleaGeneratorWithGeneratedSeed` produces a seeded pseudo-random number generator suitable for contexts where cryptographic guarantees are not required.

Sources: packages/random/jest.config.ts:L1

Two factory helpers control how seeds are supplied: `createWithSeeds` wires explicit seed values into the generator, while `safelyCreateWithSeeds` wraps that path with defensive checks before delegating. The `insecure` export is the pre-built, lazily seeded singleton intended for non-security-critical call sites.

Sources: packages/random/jest.config.ts:L1

---

The SHA-256 package is a pure-TypeScript implementation broken into focused computational primitives. `safeAdd` and the bit-rotation helpers `s` and `r` form the arithmetic core of the compression function.

Sources: packages/sha256/jest.config.ts:L1

Input text is transformed into a binary word array by `str2binb`, which handles UTF-8 boundary conditions via `utf8Encode`.

Sources: packages/sha256/src/binb2hex.ts:L1

The digest is serialized back to a human-readable form by `binb2hex`, which converts a 32-bit word array into a lowercase hexadecimal string.

Sources: packages/sha256/src/binb2hex.ts:L1

---

The base64 package provides encoding and decoding utilities in a standalone module with no runtime dependencies. Its Jest configuration confirms a server-side preset, indicating the primary consumers are backend services handling binary payloads such as file uploads and token interchange.

Sources: packages/base64/jest.config.ts:L1

---

The tools package collects small, single-responsibility utilities that do not belong to a domain-specific package.

**Stream utilities.** `streamToBuffer` consumes a `Readable` stream and resolves a `Promise<Buffer>` once the stream closes, accumulating chunks via an event listener pattern. This is the standard bridge between Node.js streaming I/O and buffer-oriented APIs.

Sources: packages/tools/src/stream.ts:L1

**Time conversion.** `convertFromDaysToMilliseconds` performs the arithmetic translation required when configuration values expressed in days must be passed to APIs that accept milliseconds.

Sources: packages/tools/src/converter.ts:L1

**Login expiration.** `getLoginExpirationInDays` and `getLoginExpirationInMs` read session-lifetime configuration and return the value in the appropriate unit, delegating the unit conversion to the converter primitive.

Sources: packages/tools/src/converter.ts:L1

**Type guards.** `isRecord` narrows an `unknown` value to `Record<string | number | symbol, unknown>`, providing a safe structural check before property access in deserialization paths.

Sources: packages/tools/src/isRecord.ts:L1

**Path flattening.** `convertSubObjectsIntoPaths` recursively transforms a nested object into a flat map of dot-notation keys, a common requirement when constructing MongoDB `$set` update documents.

Sources: packages/tools/jest.config.ts:L1

---

The JWT package provides token creation and verification primitives consumed by authentication middleware.

Sources: packages/jwt/jest.config.ts:L1

CAS validation (`pkg:cas-validate`) implements the Central Authentication Service ticket validation protocol, parsing XML responses from a CAS server and extracting principal attributes.

Sources: packages/cas-validate/jest.config.ts:L1

The server-fetch package wraps the standard `fetch` API with extended options defined in `types.ts`, notably adding SSRF-mitigation configuration to prevent server-side request forgery when making outbound HTTP calls.

Sources: packages/server-fetch/src/types.ts:L1

---

The desktop-api package exports only TypeScript type definitions and interface contracts, establishing the message-passing protocol between the Rocket.Chat web application and Electron-based desktop wrappers.

Sources: packages/desktop-api/src/index.ts:L1

Server-cloud communication types follow the same type-only philosophy, providing shared contracts for payloads exchanged between self-hosted instances and Rocket.Chat Cloud services, ensuring compile-time alignment without introducing runtime coupling.

Sources: packages/server-fetch/src/types.ts:L1

Custom Meteor Packages & Legacy Infrastr.text:
This chapter describes the collection of custom Meteor packages that form Rocket.Chat's legacy infrastructure layer. These packages handle concerns that span the full request lifecycle — from asset versioning and hot reload to cookie management, HTML injection, CSS preprocessing, and privileged database operations.

---

The autoupdate subsystem is split across two complementary modules that coordinate live client refreshes without requiring manual page reloads.

The **server-side publisher** (`autoupdate_server.js`) manages and broadcasts client version records over DDP. When a new build is deployed, it publishes updated version hashes to all connected clients, signalling whether a soft reload (asset swap) or a hard reload (full page refresh) is appropriate.

Sources: apps/meteor/packages/autoupdate/autoupdate_server.js:L1

The **client-side manager** (`autoupdate_client.js`) subscribes to these version publications. On receiving a changed version record it compares the incoming hash against the locally cached version and dispatches either a hot-code-push or a forced `window.location.reload()`. This makes the autoupdate subsystem a cross-layer dispatcher that sits on the hot path of every deployment.

Sources: apps/meteor/packages/autoupdate/autoupdate_client.js:L1

The DDP Streamer microservice exposes a parallel `Autoupdate` abstraction (`ee/apps/ddp-streamer/src/lib/Autoupdate.ts`) that replicates version state for horizontally scaled deployments, ensuring that instances behind a load balancer converge on the same client asset version.

---

The version plugin introduces a custom Meteor build step that stamps a version string directly into compiled assets.

The `package.js` manifest declares the plugin and its dependencies.

Sources: apps/meteor/packages/rocketchat-version/package.js:L1

`VersionCompiler`, defined in `compile-version.js`, implements the Meteor `Plugin.registerCompiler` interface. It reads the package's version file and emits a JavaScript module that exports the version string, making it available at runtime on both client and server without a network round-trip.

Sources: apps/meteor/packages/rocketchat-version/plugin/compile-version.js:L1

---

This package provides a mechanism to embed data directly into the initial HTML payload sent to the browser, avoiding a separate round-trip for bootstrapping critical state.

`inject-server.js` registers Meteor connect middleware that intercepts the HTML response stream. It exposes helper utilities such as `escapeReplaceString` to safely embed arbitrary JSON or script content into `<head>` or `<body>` placeholders without introducing XSS vectors.

Sources: apps/meteor/packages/meteor-inject-initial/lib/inject-server.js:L1

`inject-core.js` provides the shared API surface (registration, priority ordering, and content accumulation) that both server and client sides consume to coordinate what gets injected.

Sources: apps/meteor/packages/meteor-inject-initial/lib/inject-core.js:L1

---

This package enables server-side operations to temporarily impersonate a user context, which is essential for features like admin-initiated message edits that must pass user-level permission checks.

`collection.overwrites.js` monkey-patches the standard Meteor `Mongo.Collection` write methods (`insert`, `update`, `remove`) to propagate an ambient user identity through the call stack.

Sources: apps/meteor/packages/meteor-run-as-user/lib/collection.overwrites.js:L1

---

The PostCSS build plugin integrates CSS processing into Meteor's asset pipeline. `build.js` exposes two key responsibilities: `loadPostcssConfig` reads the project-level PostCSS configuration (plugins, autoprefixing rules, nesting support), and `isImportFile` identifies CSS files that should be treated as imports rather than standalone stylesheets, preventing duplicate output in the compiled bundle.

Sources: apps/meteor/packages/rocketchat-postcss/build.js:L1

---

The `UpdaterImpl` class in `packages/models/src/updater.ts` implements a typed builder pattern over raw MongoDB update operators (`$set`, `$unset`, `$inc`, `$addToSet`). It exposes a `hasChanges` guard that allows callers to skip no-op writes, and a `getRawUpdateFilter` method that serialises the accumulated operations into a driver-compatible document.

Sources: packages/models/src/updater.ts:L1

Together these packages form a coherent legacy infrastructure layer that underpins Rocket.Chat's Meteor-era deployment model while remaining compatible with the newer microservice topology.

File Upload, UFS & Image Processing.text:
This chapter describes the server-side architecture responsible for receiving, storing, validating, and transforming uploaded files in Rocket.Chat. The system is organized into four cooperating layers: the Unified File Store (UFS) abstraction, concrete storage back-ends, upload lifecycle methods, and an image-processing service.

---

The central coordinator is the `UploadFS` singleton, which maintains a registry of storage stores, manages MIME-type mappings, and owns the global configuration surface for all upload-related concerns.

Sources: apps/meteor/server/ufs/ufs.ts:L1

The entry point that bootstraps this subsystem re-exports the `UploadFS` singleton and eagerly loads all storage-subsystem modules so that stores are registered before any request arrives.

Sources: apps/meteor/server/ufs/index.ts:L1

Upload store settings—such as HTTPS enforcement, upload-speed simulation, storage paths, and temporary-directory permissions—are captured in a `Config` value object.

Sources: apps/meteor/server/ufs/ufs-config.ts:L1

---

The `Store` base class wires together lifecycle callbacks (before/after create, read, delete) and stream transformations, and exposes canonical operations such as `removeById`, `generateToken`, `getFilePath`, and `getFileRelativeURL`.

Sources: apps/meteor/server/ufs/ufs-store.ts:L1

Two concrete back-ends are provided:

**LocalStore** resolves uploaded files to a path on the local filesystem. Its `getFilePath` method computes the absolute location of a stored file.

Sources: apps/meteor/server/ufs/ufs-local.ts:L1

**GridFSStore** persists files directly into MongoDB GridFS, making it suitable for clustered deployments where a shared filesystem is unavailable.

Sources: apps/meteor/server/ufs/ufs-gridfs.ts:L1

---

Before a file is accepted, the `Filter` component enforces constraints on file size (min/max), allowed extensions, and permitted content types. Its `check` method is called early in the upload pipeline and throws on any violation.

Sources: apps/meteor/server/ufs/ufs-filter.ts:L1

The Uploads MongoDB model, `UploadsRaw`, backs persistent metadata storage. It provides queries such as `findNotHiddenFilesOfRoom` and `findPaginatedWithoutDirectMessages` and holds federation-aware fields for cross-server file sharing.

Sources: packages/models/src/models/Uploads.ts:L1

---

The Meteor method `ufsComplete` is called by the client after the raw bytes have been transferred. It finalises the upload record, moves the file from a temporary location to its permanent store, and triggers post-processing hooks.

Sources: apps/meteor/server/ufs/ufs-methods.ts:L1

The upload service's `parseFileIntoMessageAttachments` function translates a completed upload record into the attachment structure that will be embedded in a chat message. It handles MIME-type detection and generates thumbnail URLs.

Sources: apps/meteor/server/services/upload/service.ts:L1

File metadata sanitisation—preventing path-traversal and illegal characters—is handled by `sanitizeFileName`.

Sources: apps/meteor/app/file/server/functions/sanitizeFileName.ts:L1

The `RocketChatFile` module provides lower-level file storage and retrieval primitives shared across GridFS and filesystem paths.

Sources: apps/meteor/app/file/server/file.server.ts:L1

---

The `MediaService` encapsulates all image-manipulation logic. Its surface area includes:

- **`resizeFromBuffer` / `resizeFromStream`** – resize an image to target dimensions.
- **`isImage` / `isSvgImage`** – MIME-type probes used to gate processing steps.
- **`stripExifFromBuffer` / `stripExifFromImage`** – remove EXIF metadata before storage to protect uploader privacy.

Sources: apps/meteor/server/services/image/service.ts:L1

---

File Upload, UFS & Image Processing.section: HTTP Range Support and Content Delivery
File Upload, UFS & Image Processing.text:
Range-request semantics (required for audio/video streaming) are implemented in a dedicated module. `getByteRange` parses the `Range` header, `getFileRange` slices the underlying data source, and `setRangeHeaders` stamps the response with `Content-Range` and `Accept-Ranges` headers.

Sources: apps/meteor/app/file-upload/server/lib/ranges.ts:L1

Content-disposition behaviour—controlling whether a browser renders or downloads a file—is governed by `getContentDisposition` and the `forceDownload` helper, both of which read server settings to determine the appropriate header value.

Sources: apps/meteor/app/file-upload/server/config/helper.ts:L1

---

On the client, `createUploadsAPI` is a factory that constructs a stateful upload manager for a given chat room. It handles pre-flight validation, progress tracking, and delegates the actual transmission to the UFS layer.

Sources: apps/meteor/client/lib/chats/uploads.ts:L1

Service Workers & Public Assets.text:
This chapter documents the public-facing service worker scripts and client-side encryption worker utilities that Rocket.Chat serves directly to browsers. These components sit at the boundary between the server and the browser runtime, handling asset caching, offline resilience, and transparent decryption of encrypted file downloads.

---

The primary service worker for static asset caching is located at `apps/meteor/public/workers/index.js`. It implements a version-based cache strategy: on activation it purges stale cache buckets (identified by version hash), and on fetch it intercepts network requests to serve cached responses for known static assets. Two helper predicates, `removeHash` and `hasHash`, drive the cache-key normalization logic, stripping or detecting content-hash suffixes in asset URLs so that versioned filenames map cleanly to cache entries.

Sources: apps/meteor/public/workers/index.js:L1

The worker follows a singleton lifecycle—a single installation is shared across all tabs—and is registered from the main client bundle via `apps/meteor/client/serviceWorker.ts`, which handles both the registration handshake and the page-reload orchestration needed when a new worker version activates.

Sources: apps/meteor/client/serviceWorker.ts:L1

---

`apps/meteor/public/enc.js` is a dedicated service worker whose sole responsibility is intercepting fetch requests for encrypted file attachments and decrypting them transparently before handing the response back to the browser. It acts as an in-browser decrypt proxy: when the client posts a session key to the worker, the worker stores it in memory and uses it to decrypt streamed ciphertext on the fly. This design keeps plaintext data entirely within the browser process and off the network.

Sources: apps/meteor/public/enc.js:L1

The encryption primitives consumed by this worker are provided by the broader E2EE subsystem. AES operations (key import, encrypt, decrypt) are implemented in `apps/meteor/client/lib/e2ee/crypto/aes.ts`, and PBKDF2-based key derivation lives in `apps/meteor/client/lib/e2ee/crypto/pbkdf2.ts`.

Sources: apps/meteor/client/lib/e2ee/crypto/aes.ts:L1
Sources: apps/meteor/client/lib/e2ee/crypto/pbkdf2.ts:L1

Session key export and group-key import for individual encrypted rooms are managed by `apps/meteor/client/lib/e2ee/rocketchat.e2e.room.ts`, which exposes `exportSessionKey` and `importGroupKey`. The worker receives the exported key material through a `postMessage` channel established when a room's E2EE session is ready.

Sources: apps/meteor/client/lib/e2ee/rocketchat.e2e.room.ts:L1

---

The keychain module at `apps/meteor/client/lib/e2ee/keychain.ts` provides `decryptKey` and `decode`, which are responsible for unwrapping persisted encrypted private keys retrieved from the server. RSA asymmetric operations (key generation, public/private key import and export, encrypt/decrypt) are centralized in `apps/meteor/client/lib/e2ee/crypto/rsa.ts`.

Sources: apps/meteor/client/lib/e2ee/keychain.ts:L1
Sources: apps/meteor/client/lib/e2ee/crypto/rsa.ts:L1

Structured logging across all E2EE modules is provided by `apps/meteor/client/lib/e2ee/logger.ts`, which exposes a `createLogger` factory and a `span` helper for trace-level diagnostics.

Sources: apps/meteor/client/lib/e2ee/logger.ts:L1

---

Enterprise license validation uses a separate cryptographic pipeline in `ee/packages/license/src/token.ts`. The module exposes `decrypt`, `decryptStatsToken`, and `base64Decode`, which together verify JWT-wrapped license payloads using RSA signatures. This is distinct from the messaging E2EE stack but reuses the same underlying Web Crypto primitives available in both Node.js and browser contexts.

Sources: ee/packages/license/src/token.ts:L1

---

At runtime the asset cache worker (`workers/index.js`) and the encryption worker (`enc.js`) operate as independent service worker registrations. The asset worker intercepts navigation and static-resource fetches; the encryption worker intercepts attachment fetches. Key material flows from the E2EE room session layer into the encryption worker via `postMessage`, keeping cryptographic secrets scoped to the browser's service worker thread and never serialized to disk or sent over the network in plaintext.

Sources: apps/meteor/public/workers/index.js:L1
Sources: apps/meteor/public/enc.js:L1
Sources: apps/meteor/client/lib/e2ee/rocketchat.e2e.room.ts:L1

OAuth2 Server, Personal Access Tokens &.section: OAuth2 Server, Personal Access Tokens & Session
OAuth2 Server, Personal Access Tokens &.text:
This chapter describes the built-in OAuth2 authorization server, the OAuth application management layer, and the personal access token subsystem within Rocket.Chat's server-side architecture.

---

The core of the OAuth2 implementation lives in the server-side model layer, which implements the full authorization code and refresh token flows required by the `oauth2-server` library. The `Model` class in this file provides all persistence-backed callbacks the OAuth2 framework expects, including `getAccessToken`, `getClient`, `getAuthorizationCode`, `saveAuthorizationCode`, `saveToken`, `getRefreshToken`, and `verifyScope`.

Sources: apps/meteor/server/oauth2-server/model.ts:L1

The `getAccessToken` method resolves an opaque bearer token string against the stored token collection, returning the associated user and client. `saveToken` persists the newly issued access and refresh token pair. `getClient` validates the requesting client application by its client ID and secret, delegating to the `OAuthApps` model.

Sources: apps/meteor/server/oauth2-server/model.ts:L1

The `OAuth2Server` class in the `oauth.ts` file wraps the model and exposes the HTTP routes for the authorization, token, and decision endpoints. Its `initRoutes` method registers these routes against the Meteor/Express application and sets up the `oauth` and `config` objects that govern token lifetimes and grant types.

Sources: apps/meteor/server/oauth2-server/oauth.ts:L1

---

OAuth applications (clients) are persisted in a dedicated MongoDB collection managed by `OAuthAppsRaw`. This model provides typed query helpers including `findOneAuthAppByIdOrClientId`, `findOneActiveByClientId`, and `findOneActiveByClientIdAndClientSecret`, which are invoked during the `getClient` model callback to validate inbound authorization requests.

Sources: packages/models/src/models/OAuthApps.ts:L1

The `addOAuthApp` function in the admin functions layer handles creation of new OAuth applications, validating redirect URIs and generating the client ID and secret pair before inserting into the `OAuthApps` collection.

Sources: apps/meteor/app/oauth2-server-config/server/admin/functions/addOAuthApp.ts:L1

Redirect URI normalization is handled by `parseUriList`, a utility that sanitizes and splits the raw redirect URI string provided during application registration into a canonical list suitable for storage and later validation.

Sources: apps/meteor/app/oauth2-server-config/server/admin/functions/parseUriList.ts:L1

The `oAuth2ServerAuth` export and the `oauth2-server` configuration are assembled in the config module, which wires the `OAuth2Server` instance into the application's route tree and sets the active authorization server for the Rocket.Chat instance.

Sources: apps/meteor/app/oauth2-server-config/server/oauth/oauth2-server.ts:L1

---

Personal access tokens (PATs) allow users to authenticate API calls without a full OAuth flow. Token generation is performed by `generatePersonalAccessTokenOfUser`, which creates a hashed token record and attaches it to the user document.

Sources: apps/meteor/imports/personal-access-tokens/server/api/methods/generateToken.ts:L1

Token regeneration — invalidating the current token and issuing a replacement — is handled by `regenerateToken` and `regeneratePersonalAccessTokenOfUser`. These methods remove the existing token hash and invoke the generation logic to produce and store a fresh secret.

Sources: apps/meteor/imports/personal-access-tokens/server/api/methods/regenerateToken.ts:L1

Revocation is implemented via `removePersonalAccessTokenOfUser` on the `UsersRaw` model, which performs a targeted pull operation against the token sub-array embedded in the user document, ensuring the token is no longer accepted for authentication.

Sources: packages/models/src/models/Users.ts:L1

---

All OAuth and PAT HTTP endpoints are registered through the `APIClass` router, which provides rate-limiting, authentication middleware attachment, and the `success`/`failure` response helpers consumed uniformly across all REST endpoints in Rocket.Chat.

Sources: apps/meteor/app/api/server/ApiClass.ts:L1

---

An inbound token request travels from the HTTP route (registered in `oauth.ts`) through the `Model` callbacks, which read and write OAuth application records via `OAuthAppsRaw` and user records via `UsersRaw`. Personal access tokens bypass the OAuth grant flow entirely, relying on the user document's embedded token array, managed by the methods and model described above.

Sources: apps/meteor/server/oauth2-server/oauth.ts:L1
Sources: packages/models/src/models/OAuthApps.ts:L1
Sources: packages/models/src/models/Users.ts:L1

Engagement, NPS Surveys & Version Checks.text:
This chapter covers two distinct but related engagement subsystems: the Net Promoter Score (NPS) survey pipeline that collects workspace sentiment and reports it to Rocket.Chat cloud, and the version-check system that notifies administrators when software updates are available.

---

The NPS subsystem is responsible for scheduling surveys, collecting votes, aggregating results, and forwarding them to the cloud API. It operates as a registered microservice within the Rocket.Chat service broker.

### NPSService: Core Service Class

`NPSService` is the central service class that orchestrates the NPS lifecycle. It exposes methods including `create` (to instantiate a new survey), `vote` (to record individual responses), `closeOpenSurveys`, and `sendResults`. The `sendResults` method drives the outbound pipeline, aggregating pending votes and dispatching them.

Sources: apps/meteor/server/services/nps/service.ts:L1

### Survey Creation and Scheduling

`getAndCreateNpsSurvey` handles the logic for determining whether a new survey should be created, accepting a `NpsSurveyData` payload that describes timing and survey metadata. This function is invoked by the NPS cron scheduler.

Sources: apps/meteor/server/services/nps/getAndCreateNpsSurvey.ts:L1

The cron integration lives in a dedicated scheduler module that periodically triggers survey distribution and result processing, wiring `NPSService` methods to Rocket.Chat's server-side cron infrastructure.

Sources: apps/meteor/server/cron/nps.ts:L1

### Sending Results to Cloud

`sendNpsResults` accepts an `NPSResultPayload` — a structured object containing aggregated vote data — and submits it to the Rocket.Chat cloud API endpoint. This function is called by `NPSService.sendResults` after collecting votes from the `NpsVote` model layer.

Sources: apps/meteor/server/services/nps/sendNpsResults.ts:L1

The `NpsVoteRaw` model provides database access to individual vote records, supporting queries such as `findNotSentByNpsId` and `updateVotesToSent` which are essential for batching and marking sent results.

Sources: packages/models/src/models/NpsVote.ts:L1

The `NpsRaw` model manages the survey records themselves, with lifecycle helpers like `getOpenExpiredAndStartSending` and `updateStatusById` that control state transitions from open → sending → closed.

Sources: packages/models/src/models/Nps.ts:L1

### Admin Notification and Banners

When a survey is scheduled, administrators are informed via banners. `getBannerForAdmins` constructs the banner payload describing an upcoming NPS survey, while `notifyAdmins` delivers that notification through the Banner service to all users with administrator privileges.

Sources: apps/meteor/server/services/nps/notification.ts:L1

### Service Registration

`NPSService` is registered during server startup alongside all other microservices in the central startup bootstrapper, making it available through the service broker for inter-service calls.

Sources: apps/meteor/server/services/startup.ts:L1

---

The version-check subsystem periodically queries the Rocket.Chat cloud for available updates and surfaces actionable notifications to administrators.

### Update Discovery

`getNewUpdates` fetches available version updates from the cloud update server, sending workspace and system metadata as part of the request. This function forms the data-fetching layer at the top of the version-check pipeline.

Sources: apps/meteor/app/version-check/server/functions/getNewUpdates.ts:L1

### Processing and Message Construction

`checkVersionUpdate` coordinates the overall update-check flow, and `getMessagesToSendToAdmins` translates raw update data into structured admin messages. `showAlertsFromCloud` handles cloud-originated alert payloads that may accompany version data.

Sources: apps/meteor/app/version-check/server/functions/checkVersionUpdate.ts:L1

`buildVersionUpdateMessage` composes the actual notification messages posted to admin channels when an update is detected. It also includes `cleanupOutdatedVersionUpdateBanners`, which removes stale banners when updates have been superseded by newer releases.

Sources: apps/meteor/app/version-check/server/functions/buildVersionUpdateMessage.ts:L1

### Scheduling and Dismissal

The version-check job is registered via `addVersionCheckJob`, which attaches a periodic cron task to poll for updates on a configured interval.

Sources: apps/meteor/app/version-check/server/index.ts:L1

Administrators can dismiss version-check banners through the `banner_dismiss` server method, which marks the banner as read for the requesting user, preventing repeat display without removing the underlying record.

Sources: apps/meteor/app/version-check/server/methods/banner_dismiss.ts:L1

---

Both subsystems follow a poll-and-notify pattern: a scheduler fires periodically, a cloud query or aggregation runs, results are transformed into messages or banners, and admin users receive targeted notifications. The NPS pipeline additionally persists vote state transitions in MongoDB before forwarding batched results to the cloud, ensuring reliable at-least-once delivery semantics through status-flag updates on `NpsVote` records.

Emoji, Custom Sounds & Custom Status.text:
This chapter describes how Rocket.Chat implements emoji registration, EmojiOne configuration, custom emoji lifecycle management, custom notification sounds, and custom user status. These features share a common pattern: a registry or data model on the server, a client-side event/render pipeline, and Meteor methods bridging the two.

---

The core emoji subsystem is built around two complementary registries — one for the server and one for the client. Both expose a typed extension point described by `EmojiPackage` and `EmojiPackages`, which define the shape of an emoji provider (name, render function, picker configuration, and category list).

Sources: apps/meteor/app/emoji/lib/rocketchat.ts:L1

The **server-side registry** (`apps/meteor/app/emoji/server/lib.ts`) exports the authoritative package map and base configuration used during server startup. Packages register themselves into this map, making their emoji sets available for later lookup.

Sources: apps/meteor/app/emoji/server/lib.ts:L1

The **client-side registry** (`apps/meteor/app/emoji/client/lib.ts`) mirrors this structure and additionally exposes `emojiEmitter`, an event dispatcher that coordinates rendering requests across different emoji packages. When a message is rendered, the emitter fires events that registered packages respond to, allowing EmojiOne and custom emoji packages to coexist transparently.

Sources: apps/meteor/app/emoji/client/lib.ts:L1

---

The `emojiParser` module (`apps/meteor/app/emoji/client/emojiParser.ts`) is the hot-path entry point for converting raw emoji shortcodes (e.g., `:smile:`) into HTML representations. It scans message strings, identifies shortcode tokens, queries the active emoji packages for a match, and replaces tokens with either image tags or Unicode characters depending on the matched package's render function.

Sources: apps/meteor/app/emoji/client/emojiParser.ts:L1

Helper utilities in `apps/meteor/app/emoji/client/helpers.ts` support the emoji picker UI by organizing emoji into categories, managing recency lists, and generating row structures for virtualized rendering. The `CUSTOM_CATEGORY` constant separates user-uploaded emoji from system sets.

Sources: apps/meteor/app/emoji/client/helpers.ts:L1

At the Gazzodown rendering layer, the `Emoji` React component (`packages/gazzodown/src/emoji/Emoji.tsx`) consumes parsed emoji tokens from the message AST and renders them with optional size and preview overrides, acting as the final display boundary.

Sources: packages/gazzodown/src/emoji/Emoji.tsx:L1

---

The `getEmojiConfig` factory (`apps/meteor/app/emoji-emojione/lib/getEmojiConfig.ts`) constructs and patches the EmojiOne library instance. It applies Rocket.Chat-specific rendering overrides (CDN paths, image formats, sprite vs. individual-image mode) and exposes `isEmojiSupported` to gate rendering based on the current configuration. The `isSetNotNull` guard utility (`apps/meteor/app/emoji-emojione/lib/isSetNotNull.ts`) is used internally to validate that async configuration lookups return meaningful values before patching proceeds.

Sources: apps/meteor/app/emoji-emojione/lib/getEmojiConfig.ts:L1
Sources: apps/meteor/app/emoji-emojione/lib/isSetNotNull.ts:L1

---

Custom emoji follow a clear server-side lifecycle: upload → insert/update → delete.

**Upload** is handled by `uploadEmojiCustomWithBuffer` in `apps/meteor/app/emoji-custom/server/lib/uploadEmojiCustom.ts`, which validates file type and size, checks caller permissions, and writes the file through the UFS store layer.

Sources: apps/meteor/app/emoji-custom/server/lib/uploadEmojiCustom.ts:L1

**Insert and update** operations flow through `apps/meteor/app/emoji-custom/server/methods/insertOrUpdateEmoji.ts`, which delegates to the `insertOrUpdateEmoji` server library. That library defines `EmojiData` and `EmojiDataWithParsedAliases` types, parses comma-separated alias strings into arrays, validates uniqueness against `EmojiCustom` model queries, and persists records.

Sources: apps/meteor/app/emoji-custom/server/methods/insertOrUpdateEmoji.ts:L1

The `EmojiCustom` model (`packages/models/src/models/EmojiCustom.ts`) provides the data access layer, exposing `findByNameOrAlias`, `findByNameOrAliasExceptID`, and field setters used by the server library.

Sources: packages/models/src/models/EmojiCustom.ts:L1

**Client-side operations** (`apps/meteor/client/lib/customEmoji.ts`) implement `updateEmojiCustom`, `deleteEmojiCustom`, and `customRender`, synchronizing the local emoji registry after server acknowledgment and handling the client rendering of custom emoji images.

Sources: apps/meteor/client/lib/customEmoji.ts:L1

---

Custom notification sounds follow a parallel pattern to custom emoji. The `ICustomSoundData` type and `insertOrUpdateSound` method (`apps/meteor/app/custom-sounds/server/methods/insertOrUpdateSound.ts`) define the data contract and persistence logic for sound records. Upload, validation, and storage mirror the emoji upload flow, relying on the same UFS-based infrastructure.

Sources: apps/meteor/app/custom-sounds/server/methods/insertOrUpdateSound.ts:L1

---

Client-side custom status management is centralized in `apps/meteor/client/lib/userStatuses.ts`, which implements a `UserStatuses` singleton registry. It exposes `createFromCustom`, `put`, `delete`, and `sync` operations, and uses `watch` to subscribe to real-time server changes. The registry validates status types via `isValidType` before committing updates, ensuring only recognized status values propagate to the presence system.

Sources: apps/meteor/client/lib/userStatuses.ts:L1

Outlook Calendar Integration & Status Sy.text:
This chapter describes the architecture of Rocket.Chat's Outlook Calendar integration, covering the client-side OAuth authentication hooks, desktop-specific error handling, event modal UI, and the server-side cron-based status synchronization pipeline.

---

The Outlook Calendar integration allows users to synchronize their Outlook calendar events with Rocket.Chat, automatically reflecting meeting statuses and enabling in-app call joining directly from calendar events. The feature is split between a client-side view layer (React hooks, modals, and event list components) and a server-side service layer responsible for scheduling and applying status changes.

---

The integration explicitly targets the Rocket.Chat desktop application. When a user attempts to use calendar features outside of a supported desktop context, a dedicated `NotOnDesktopError` is thrown.

`NotOnDesktopError` is a typed error class that signals to the calling code that the Outlook calendar workflow requires the desktop client.

Sources: apps/meteor/client/views/outlookCalendar/lib/NotOnDesktopError.ts:L1

This pattern follows the broader Rocket.Chat client-side error hierarchy, where specialized subclasses of a base error type (such as `RocketChatError`) carry typed context for controlled UI error handling.

Sources: apps/meteor/client/lib/errors/RocketChatError.ts:L1

---

Authentication with Outlook is managed via two cooperating React hooks defined in a single module:

- **`useOutlookAuthenticationMutation`** encapsulates the async mutation logic for initiating or refreshing an Outlook OAuth handshake. It is the low-level primitive that performs the actual credential request.
- **`useOutlookAuthentication`** composes over `useOutlookAuthenticationMutation`, providing a higher-level interface for components that need to trigger authentication and respond to success or failure states.

Both hooks are co-located and exported from the same file, reflecting a pattern where mutation primitives and their composed consumer hooks are kept together for cohesion.

Sources: apps/meteor/client/views/outlookCalendar/hooks/useOutlookAuthentication.ts:L1

---

The `OutlookCalendarEventModal` component presents event details to the user, such as meeting title, time, and attendees, inside a Rocket.Chat modal dialog. It accepts `OutlookCalendarEventModalProps` to receive the event data and callback handlers.

Sources: apps/meteor/client/views/outlookCalendar/OutlookCalendarEventModal.tsx:L1

This modal is typically triggered from the event list, providing a focal point for user interaction with a specific calendar event.

---

The `OutlookEventItem` component renders a single calendar event row within the event list. It accepts `OutlookEventItemProps` and exposes a `handleOpenEvent` handler that responds to user interaction by either opening the event modal or initiating a call.

Sources: apps/meteor/client/views/outlookCalendar/OutlookEventsList/OutlookEventItem.tsx:L1

Call-joining behavior is provided by the `useOutlookOpenCall` hook, which abstracts the logic for resolving a call URL from an event and triggering the appropriate VoIP or video call flow.

Sources: apps/meteor/client/views/outlookCalendar/hooks/useOutlookOpenCall.ts:L1

---

On the server, Rocket.Chat uses a cron-based pipeline to apply calendar event status changes automatically.

**`generateCronJobId`** is a utility function that produces a deterministic, unique identifier for each scheduled status-change cron job, ensuring idempotent job registration and deduplication across server restarts.

Sources: apps/meteor/server/services/calendar/statusEvents/generateCronJobId.ts:L1

**`cancelUpcomingStatusChanges`** is a service method responsible for removing any pending scheduled status updates—for example, when a user's meeting is cancelled or their calendar is re-synced. This prevents stale status changes from being applied after the underlying event has changed.

Sources: apps/meteor/server/services/calendar/service.ts:L1

**`applyStatusChange`** contains the logic (exercised under test) for transitioning a user's Rocket.Chat status in response to a calendar event becoming active or ending.

Sources: apps/meteor/tests/unit/server/services/calendar/statusEvents/applyStatusChange.ts:L1

The calendar event data model backing this pipeline provides database operations for querying and updating event records, including external ID lookups and notification tracking.

Sources: packages/models/src/models/CalendarEvent.ts:L1

---

The end-to-end flow proceeds as follows: the client authenticates via OAuth hooks → calendar events are fetched and displayed via `OutlookEventItem` → a user can open a call with `useOutlookOpenCall` → on the server, cron jobs identified by `generateCronJobId` fire at event boundaries, calling `applyStatusChange` to update user status, with `cancelUpcomingStatusChanges` cleaning up invalidated jobs when events are removed or modified.

Invite Links, Conference Pages & Error P.section: Invite Links, Conference Pages & Error Pages
Invite Links, Conference Pages & Error P.text:
This chapter covers three distinct but related UI subsystems: the invite link flow (including SAML token integration), the video conference landing page, and the generic error pages for not-found and not-authorized states. Together these modules handle the edges of user entry into Rocket.Chat — joining via external link, joining a call, or encountering access boundaries.

---

The invite subsystem allows users to enter a workspace or room via a time-limited URL. The entry point is `InvitePage`, which orchestrates token validation and room joining, and `SecretURLPage`, which handles secret-URL-based registration paths.

Sources: apps/meteor/client/views/invite/hooks/useSamlInviteToken.ts:L1

### SAML Token Persistence

`useSamlInviteToken` is a React hook responsible for retrieving and managing SAML invite tokens from session storage. When a user arrives via an invite link that requires SAML authentication, the token must survive the redirect cycle. This hook reads the token before the SAML redirect, stores it in session storage, and restores it after the authentication round-trip completes, ensuring the invite context is not lost during SSO flows.

Sources: apps/meteor/client/views/invite/hooks/useSamlInviteToken.ts:L1

### Token Validation and Consumption

`useValidateInviteQuery` performs a server query to verify that an invite token is still valid (not expired, not over its usage limit). This query result gates whether the invite UI proceeds to the join step or surfaces an error state.

Sources: apps/meteor/client/views/invite/hooks/useSamlInviteToken.ts:L1

`useInviteTokenMutation` wraps the server-side token consumption call. Once a user confirms they wish to join, this mutation is fired to register the use of the token and add the user to the target room. Error and success states from this mutation drive the UI feedback presented in `InvitePage`.

Sources: apps/meteor/client/views/invite/hooks/useSamlInviteToken.ts:L1

### Route-Level SAML Integration

`SAMLLoginRoute` coordinates SAML-based login at the router level, and interacts with the SAML invite token mechanism so that users arriving via invite links are correctly redirected post-authentication.

Sources: apps/meteor/client/views/invite/hooks/useSamlInviteToken.ts:L1

---

The conference subsystem provides a standalone landing page for users joining a video call, decoupled from the main room view.

### ConferencePage

`ConferencePage` is the primary React component for this subsystem. It reads query parameters (via `getQueryParams`) from the URL to extract the conference identifier and relevant metadata, then manages the video call state — loading, active, or error — and handles navigation once the call ends.

Sources: apps/meteor/client/views/conference/ConferencePage.tsx:L1

### ConferencePageError

`ConferencePageError` is a dedicated error display component rendered when the conference cannot be joined — for example, when the call has ended or the link is invalid. It renders localized, user-friendly error messages and provides navigation options to return to the workspace.

Sources: apps/meteor/client/views/conference/ConferencePageError.tsx:L1

### ConferenceRoute

`ConferenceRoute` is the router-level entry point that maps the conference URL pattern to `ConferencePage`. It serves as the boundary between the application router and the conference UI subtree.

Sources: apps/meteor/client/views/conference/ConferenceRoute.tsx:L1

---

### NotFoundPage

`NotFoundPage` is the generic 404 component displayed when a route or resource cannot be resolved. It provides a consistent visual treatment for missing content and typically includes a link back to the workspace home.

Sources: apps/meteor/client/views/conference/ConferencePage.tsx:L1

### NotAuthorizedPage

`NotAuthorizedPage` handles access-denied scenarios — situations where the user is authenticated but lacks permission to view the requested resource. It is accompanied by a Storybook file (`NotAuthorizedPage.stories`) that documents its visual variants and states for design-system consistency.

Sources: apps/meteor/client/views/conference/ConferencePageError.tsx:L1

---

Route parameter access throughout these modules relies on `useRouteParameter`, a hook from the `ui-contexts` package that provides a typed interface for reading named parameters from the active route without direct router coupling.
